title: Generic Types and Classes
summary: Give type aliases, interfaces, and classes their own type parameters, and type the generic built-ins Map, Set, and Node's EventEmitter.
intro: Functions aren't the only things that take type parameters. A response wrapper, a page of results, a repository, or a cache has the same shape whatever it holds, so you write the shape once with a type parameter and fill it in at each use: `Page<Product>`, `TtlCache<string, number>`. In this lesson you write generic type aliases, interfaces, and classes, give type parameters defaults, and type the generic built-ins you'll meet in every codebase: `Map`, `Set`, and Node's `EventEmitter`.

steps.title: Generic type aliases and interfaces

examples.title: An API response
examples.prompt: Wrap a user and a list of users in the same response type with one generic `respond`.
examples.explanation: `ApiResponse<T>` describes every response at once, and each use fills in `T`. `respond` is a generic function whose return type is the generic type, so each call's `T` flows from its argument into its result. `respond(ada)` returns an `ApiResponse<User>`, whose `data` is a `User`, and `respond(users)` returns an `ApiResponse<User[]>`, whose `data` you can `map`. The bubbles show each type with its argument filled in, which reads like a sentence: an API response of users.

examples.title: Pages and a default
examples.prompt: Describe pages of results with `Page<T>`, and wrap responses in an `Envelope` whose type argument has a default.
examples.output:
Mug, Kettle (next: c2)
Teapot (next: none)
200: 2 items
500: Server error
examples.explanation: `Page<T>` fits a page of anything: `Page<string>` here, `Page<Order>` elsewhere, with `nextCursor` set to `null` on the last page. Type arguments nest, so `Envelope<Page<string>>` is an envelope whose body is a page of strings, and `ok.body.items` is typed all the way down. `Envelope` has a default, so `failed: Envelope` means `Envelope<unknown>`, as the bubble shows. Its body could be anything, so the code checks `typeof failed.body === "string"` before printing it. Without the default, `Envelope` alone would be the TS2314 error.

examples.title: A repository interface
examples.prompt: Write one `Repository<T>` interface, build a repository of books and one of members from arrays, and print both with one function.
examples.output:
Books: Dune, Emma
Members: Ada
Emma
no such book
examples.explanation: An interface takes type parameters just like a type alias, and its methods use them: for a `Repository<Book>`, `get` returns `Book | undefined` and `list` returns `Book[]`. `arrayRepo` builds one from any array of items that have an `id`, and the object it returns gets its method types from the return type, so `(id) => ...` needs no annotation. For `members`, `arrayRepo<Member>` writes the type argument out, so the array literal is checked against `Member` as you type it. `report` takes any `Repository<T>`, and its `show` callback gets the right item type for each repository. Code written against the interface doesn't care where the items live: an array here, a database later.

practice.title: Paginate
practice.prompt:
Write a generic `paginate` that cuts one page out of any list and says where the next page starts.

1. Make the exported `Page` type generic: `type Page<T> = { items: T[]; nextCursor: string | null }`.
2. Give `paginate` a type parameter `T`, the parameters `items: readonly T[]`, `pageSize: number`, and `page: number` (counting from 1), and the return type `Page<T>`.
3. Return that page's items, with `nextCursor` set to the next page's number as a string, or `null` when no items come after this page.
4. Print page 3 the same way as page 1.
5. Keep the `export`s: hidden type tests import `paginate` and `Page`, and Check also pages through other lists.

Expected output:

```text
Page 1: plan sprint, write spec, review PR (next: 2)
Page 3: update docs (next: none)
```

tests.output:
Page 1: plan sprint, write spec, review PR (next: 2)
Page 3: update docs (next: none)

Page 1: plan sprint, write spec, review PR (next: 2)
Page 3: update docs (next: none)
10+20 2
30+40 null

cases.name: a page of strings isn't a page of numbers
the cursor is a string or null

hints: Write the type first, `export type Page<T> = { items: T[]; nextCursor: string | null }`. Then `paginate` returns `Page<T>`, the way `respond` returns `ApiResponse<T>` in the first example.
Page `page` starts at index `(page - 1) * pageSize`, and `items.slice(start, start + pageSize)` cuts it out. `slice` stops at the end of the array.
There's a next page when `start + pageSize < items.length`. Then `nextCursor` is `String(page + 1)`, and otherwise it's `null`.

steps.title: Generic classes

examples.title: A typed stack
examples.prompt: Keep an undo history in a stack of strings, and zoom levels in a stack of numbers, with one generic `Stack` class.
examples.output:
Undo: delete line
Undo: bold title
Next undo: nothing left
Zoomed out from 150% to 100%
examples.explanation: `new Stack<string>()` sets `T` to `string` for that stack, so `push` takes only strings, and `undo.push(42)` is a type error (TS2345). The constructor takes no item, so there's nothing to infer `T` from, and the type argument is how you say what the stack holds. `pop` and `peek` return `T | undefined` because the stack may be empty: after two undos, `peek` finds nothing, and `??` supplies the fallback. `#items` is a JavaScript private field: code outside the class can't read or change it.

examples.title: A cache with a fake clock
examples.prompt: Cache exchange rates for 60 seconds in a `TtlCache<K, V>` that reads the time from a clock function you pass in.
examples.output:
At 0 ms: 1.08
At 59999 ms: 1.08
At 60000 ms: expired
GBP: never cached
examples.explanation: `TtlCache<K, V>` has two type parameters, one for its keys and one for its values, and `new TtlCache<string, number>(...)` sets both: `set` takes a string and a number, and `get` returns `number | undefined`. The cache never reads the real time. It calls the `now` function it was given, so the program passes a fake clock and moves it forward by hand, and the rate expires at exactly 60000 ms on every run. In real code you'd pass `() => Date.now()`. Passing in what varies, instead of reaching for it inside the class, is what makes time-based code testable.

practice.title: Queue
practice.prompt:
Make `Queue` generic, so it holds items of any one type and serves them first in, first out.

1. Give `Queue` a type parameter `T`, and keep its items in a `#items: T[]` field that starts empty.
2. `enqueue(x: T): void` adds `x` at the back, and `size(): number` returns how many items are waiting.
3. `dequeue(): T | undefined` removes and returns the item at the front, or `undefined` when the queue is empty.
4. Create `tickets` as a `new Queue<string>()`.
5. Keep the `export`: hidden type tests import `Queue`, and Check also runs a queue of numbers.

Expected output:

```text
Waiting: 3
Serving T-1
Serving T-2
Waiting: 2
Serving T-3
Serving T-4
Next: nobody
```

dequeue returns the item type

hints: Follow `Stack` from the first example: `class Queue<T>` with `#items: T[] = []`, and `T` wherever the starter says `string`.
`push` adds at the back of an array, and `shift` removes and returns its first item, or `undefined` when the array is empty.
`size` returns `this.#items.length`. Write `new Queue<string>()`, because the constructor takes no item that `T` could be inferred from.

steps.title: Map, Set, and typed events

examples.title: Scores and tags
examples.prompt: Group test scores per student in a `Map`, and collect the distinct tags of some posts in a `Set`.
examples.output:
Ana: 91, 85
Ben: 78, 82
Caro: 88
4 tags: ts, types, node, zod
Has node: true
examples.explanation: `new Map<string, number[]>()` starts empty, so the type arguments say what it will hold: student names mapped to lists of scores. `get` returns `number[] | undefined`, as the bubble shows, because a student may not be in the map yet, so the loop checks before it pushes. Looping over a `Map` gives `[key, value]` pairs in the order the keys were first set. `new Set<string>()` keeps one copy of each tag, also in first-seen order, and `has` says whether a value is in it. Both start empty here, which is exactly when the type arguments are needed.

examples.title: Typed events
examples.prompt: Announce created and cancelled orders on an `EventEmitter` typed with a map of its events.
examples.output:
Created o1: $12.99
Created o2: $4.50
Cancelled o1: out of stock
examples.explanation: `OrderEvents` maps each event name to the arguments its listeners get, written as a named tuple. Passing it to `EventEmitter` types `on` and `emit` from it: the `created` listener's `order` is an `Order`, as the bubble shows, and the `cancelled` listener gets two strings, with no annotations. `emit` calls the listeners for that event right away, in the order they were added, so each line prints as its event is emitted.

examples.title: Wrong arguments
examples.prompt: Emit a `cancelled` event without its reason, and read the error.
examples.output: main.ts(13,8): error TS2554: Expected 3 arguments, but got 2.

practice.title: Order events
practice.prompt:
Type an event bus for orders, so every listener and every `emit` gets the right arguments.

1. Make the exported `OrderEvents` map two events: `placed` to `[id: string, totalCents: number]`, and `shipped` to `[id: string, carrier: string]`.
2. Pass `OrderEvents` as the type argument of the exported `bus`.
3. Add a listener for `shipped` that prints `Shipped <id> with <carrier>`.
4. Keep the `export`s: hidden type tests import `bus`, and Check also emits other events.

Expected output:

```text
Placed o1: $12.99
Placed o2: $45.00
Shipped o1 with UPS
```

tests.output:
Placed o1: $12.99
Placed o2: $45.00
Shipped o1 with UPS

Placed o1: $12.99
Placed o2: $45.00
Shipped o1 with UPS
Shipped o2 with DHL
Placed o3: $0.05

cases.name: a placed listener gets a number total
cases.code: bus.on("placed", (id: string, total: string) => console.log(id, total));

hints: Each event maps to a named tuple of its arguments, like `cancelled: [id: string, reason: string]` in the examples.
Write `new EventEmitter<OrderEvents>()`. Then the listeners' parameters get their types from the map, with no annotations.
The new listener is `bus.on("shipped", (id, carrier) => { ... })`, and it prints a template string with `id` and `carrier`.

recap:
- Type aliases and interfaces take type parameters after their name, and each use fills them in: `Page<Order>`, `Repository<Book>`.
- A generic type written without its type arguments is an error (TS2314), unless its type parameters have defaults like `<T = unknown>`.
- A generic function that returns a generic type, like `respond<T>(data: T): ApiResponse<T>`, lets callers skip writing `T`.
- A generic class takes type parameters after its name. Its constructor's arguments infer them, or you write them, as in `new Stack<string>()`.
- Keep a class's state in `#private` fields, and pass in what varies, like a clock, so its behavior is deterministic and testable.
- `Map<K, V>` and `Set<T>` are generic classes, and `Map.get` returns `V | undefined` because a key may be missing.
- `new EventEmitter<Events>()` types `on` and `emit` from a map of event names to argument tuples, but it still accepts names that aren't in the map.
